quote: I often say, when I make these little observations, ‘Had Aristotle cooked, he would have written a great deal more.’
source: Sor Juana Inés de la Cruz, The Answer, on the philosophies of the kitchen, p. 75 (trans. Electa Arenal and Amanda Powell, 1994)

evidence.where: Julie Bokser, Sor Juana's Rhetoric of Silence, Rhetoric Review 25:1 (2006), block quotes the passage in full from The Answer / La respuesta and cites page 75: But in truth, my Lady, what can we women know, save philosophies of the kitchen? It was well put by Lupercio Leonardo that one can philosophize quite well while preparing supper. I often say, when I make these little observations, followed by the Aristotle sentence. The article's other page citations, 49, 51, 73, 75, 77, track the Arenal and Powell bilingual text. The Internet Archive scans are lending restricted and could not be searched inside; the printed page was not seen.
evidence.edition: The Answer / La Respuesta, ed. and trans. Electa Arenal and Amanda Powell (The Feminist Press at CUNY, 1994), facing pages 74 and 75
evidence.locator: In the passage on the secrets of nature learned while cooking, a few lines after what can we women know, save philosophies of the kitchen

reason: The sentence is genuine and famous, and the Arenal and Powell wording is attested to the letter, with the framing clause intact, in a peer reviewed article that cites their page 75. Confidence is medium because that attestation is one scholar quoting the page rather than the page itself, and a graduate thesis citing the same edition at 74 to 75 renders the clause as if Aristotle had cooked, which reads like an adaptation to its own sentence. Other translations differ plainly: Kirk Rappaport 2005 has written much more, Grossman 2014 has I say that if Aristotle had cooked. The inner quotation keeps the proposal's single curly marks, since the printed edition's marks were not seen. Sor Juana is new to the year, and she is a woman, a 17th century voice and a Mexican one, all of which the month needs.
